claim: Auditory deprivation in the form of deafness during development leads to lasting changes in central auditory system function.
source: Auditory deprivation in the form of deafness during development leads to lasting changes in central auditory system function.
evidence: This is a general statement in the introduction that is supported by the citations that follow in the manuscript.

claim: Animal studies have shown marked differences in the anatomy, physiology, and functionality of the central auditory pathway following cochlear ablation, pharmacological neonatal deafening, and congenital deafness.
source: Animal studies have shown marked differences in the anatomy, physiology, and functionality of the central auditory pathway following cochlear ablation, pharmacological neonatal deafening, and congenital deafness (Shepherd and Hardie, 2001; Berger et al., 2017; see Butler and Lomber, 2013, for a review).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Deafness-induced changes have been identified in humans, including degeneration of spiral ganglion cells in the cochlea following congenital profound sensorineural hearing loss.
source: Deafness-induced changes have also been identified in humans, namely, degeneration of spiral ganglion cells in the cochlea (Nadol et al., 1989)
evidence: Supported by citation to Nadol et al., 1989.

claim: Congenital profound sensorineural hearing loss leads to a reduction of volume of neurons in the cochlear nucleus in humans.
source: a reduction of volume of neurons in the cochlear nucleus (Seldon and Clark, 1991; Chao et al., 2002)
evidence: Supported by citations to Seldon and Clark, 1991 and Chao et al., 2002.

claim: Congenital profound sensorineural hearing loss leads to functional reorganisation of cortical activity in humans.
source: a functional reorganisation of cortical activity (Neville et al., 1998) following congenital profound (>95 dB HL) sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neville et al., 1998.

claim: Much less is known about the effects of mild-to-moderate sensorineural hearing loss on the developing auditory pathway compared to deafness.
source: However, in contrast to the literature on deafness, much less is known about the effects of mild- (21–40 dB HL) to-moderate (41–70 dB HL; British Society of Audiology, 2011) SNHL (MMHL) on the developing auditory pathway.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, indicating a gap in knowledge.

claim: There is evidence that even transient or mild levels of hearing loss during a critical period can lead to lasting effects in the central and peripheral auditory system.
source: Nonetheless, there is evidence to suggest that even transient or mild levels of hearing loss during a critical period can lead to lasting effects in the central and peripheral auditory system (e.g. Gravel et al., 2006; Rosen et al., 2012; Takesian et al., 2012; Liberman et al., 2015; Mowery et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: At Time 1, younger children with MMHL (8–12 years) showed age-appropriate mismatch negativities (MMNs) to sounds.
source: At Time 1, younger children with MMHL (8–12 years; n = 23) showed age-appropriate mismatch negativities (MMNs) to sounds
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: At Time 1, older children with MMHL (12–16 years) did not show age-appropriate mismatch negativities (MMNs) to sounds.
source: but older children (12–16 years; n = 23) did not.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Children with MMHL who had shown significant MMNs at Time 1 showed MMNs that were reduced at Time 2 (six years later).
source: Children who had shown significant MMNs at Time 1 showed MMNs that were reduced and, for nonspeech, absent at Time 2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the longitudinal study's data analysis.

claim: Children with MMHL who had shown significant MMNs to nonspeech at Time 1 showed absent MMNs to nonspeech at Time 2 (six years later).
source: Children who had shown significant MMNs at Time 1 showed MMNs that were reduced and, for nonspeech, absent at Time 2.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the longitudinal study's data analysis.

claim: Even a mild-to-moderate hearing loss during early-to-mid childhood can lead to changes in the neural processing of sounds in late childhood/adolescence.
source: Our findings demonstrate that even a mild-to-moderate hearing loss during early-to-mid childhood can lead to changes in the neural processing of sounds in late childhood/adolescence.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The structure and function of the adult auditory system is dependent upon stimulation received during maturation.
source: The structure and function of the adult auditory system is dependent upon stimulation received during maturation (Kral and Sharma, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kral and Sharma, 2012.

claim: Late auditory evoked responses (LAERs) comprise the P1, N1, P2, and N2 components.
source: Of particular interest are the late auditory evoked responses (LAERs), comprising the P1, N1, P2, and N2 components
evidence: This is established knowledge about the components of LAERs.

claim: Mismatch responses (MMRs) comprise the mismatch negativity (MMN) and late discriminatory negativity (LDN).
source: and the mismatch responses (MMRs), comprising the mismatch negativity (MMN) and late discriminatory negativity (LDN).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the components of MMRs.

claim: The LAERs are thought to mark the initial detection (P1, N1, and P2), classification and discrimination (P2 and N2) of an auditory stimulus.
source: The LAERs are thought to mark the initial detection (P1, N1, and P2), classification and discrimination (P2 and N2) of an auditory stimulus (for a review, see Eggermont and Ponton, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to a review by Eggermont and Ponton, 2002.

claim: The MMRs are thought to reflect the discrimination of one or more different sounds.
source: In contrast, the MMRs are thought to reflect the discrimination of one or more different sounds
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of MMRs.

claim: Both the LAERs and the MMRs show distinct postnatal maturational time courses.
source: Both the LAERs and the MMRs show distinct postnatal maturational time courses (for reviews, see Gomot et al., 2000; Ponton et al., 2000a; Bishop et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple reviews.

claim: LAERs and MMRs have been identified as useful candidates to assess the effects of SNHL on the development of the auditory pathway in children.
source: Therefore, these responses have been identified as useful candidates to assess the effects of SNHL on the development of the auditory pathway in children.
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of LAERs and MMRs described in the preceding text.

claim: There is evidence that auditory cortical responses may be delayed and/or deviant in children with severe or profound SNHL.
source: There is now an abundance of evidence to suggest that auditory cortical responses may be delayed and/or deviant in children with severe or profound SNHL (Ponton et al., 1996a; Ponton et al., 1996b; Ponton et al., 1999; Ponton et al., 2000b; Ponton and Eggermont, 2001; Sharma et al., 2002; Sharma et al., 2005; see Näätänen et al., 2017, for a review of the MMN).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Ponton et al. (1996b) examined the development of the P1-N1-P2 complex in children with early-onset profound SNHL who had been fitted with unilateral cochlear implants.
source: Ponton et al. (1996b) used a combined cross-sectional and longitudinal design to examine the development of the P1-N1-P2 complex in a group of six, 6–16 year-old children with early-onset profound SNHL who had been fitted with unilateral cochlear implants (CIs) following an average period of deafness of 4.5 years (range: 1.5 to 6 years).
evidence: This describes the methods and participants of a cited study.

claim: For the youngest children (aged 5–7 years) with cochlear implants, the ERPs were very similar to those of normally hearing controls.
source: For the youngest children (aged 5–7 years), the ERPs of the CI group were very similar to those of controls, being dominated by a large P1 around 140 ms after stimulus onset, followed by a prolonged negativity (N2).
evidence: This describes findings from Ponton et al. (1996b).

claim: For older children (8–16 years) with cochlear implants, marked morphological differences in ERPs emerged compared to normally hearing controls.
source: However, for the older children (8–16 years), marked morphological differences between groups emerged: Whereas older NH controls developed an N1 response, children with CIs generally did not.
evidence: This describes findings from Ponton et al. (1996b).

claim: Older children with cochlear implants generally did not develop an N1 response, whereas older normally hearing controls did.
source: Whereas older NH controls developed an N1 response, children with CIs generally did not.
evidence: This describes findings from Ponton et al. (1996b).

claim: The ERPs of older children with cochlear implants more closely resembled those of younger normally hearing controls.
source: Instead, the ERPs of older children with CIs more closely resembled those of younger NH controls.
evidence: This describes findings from Ponton et al. (1996b).

claim: P1 was found to emerge following cochlear implantation, albeit with a latency delay proportional to the period of deafness.
source: P1 was found to emerge following implantation, albeit with a latency delay proportional to the period of deafness.
evidence: This describes findings from Ponton et al. (1999) and Ponton et al. (2000b).

claim: The MMN was robustly present in children with cochlear implants who showed good spoken language perception.
source: Moreover, the MMN was robustly present in children with CIs who showed good spoken language perception (Ponton et al., 2000b).
evidence: This describes findings from Ponton et al. (2000b).

claim: N1 was absent from almost all of the profoundly deaf children tested by Ponton and colleagues.
source: However, particularly striking was the absence of an N1 from almost all of the profoundly deaf children Ponton and colleagues had tested.
evidence: This describes findings from studies by Ponton and colleagues.

claim: Ponton and Eggermont (2001) argued that the absence of N1 provided evidence for a persistent immaturity in layer II of primary auditory cortex for children with congenital profound SNHL who were fitted with CIs.
source: Ponton and Eggermont (2001) argued that this provided evidence for a persistent immaturity in layer II of primary auditory cortex for children with congenital profound SNHL who were fitted (albeit often late) with CIs.
evidence: This describes the interpretation of findings by Ponton and Eggermont (2001).

claim: Singh et al. (2004) measured the P1-N2 and MMN responses to /ba/-/da/ of 35, 7- to 17-year-old children with bilateral profound SNHL who had been fitted with CIs between 1 and 10 years.
source: More recently, Singh et al. (2004) measured the P1-N2 and MMN responses to /ba/-/da/ of 35, 7- to 17-year-old children with bilateral profound SNHL who had been fitted with CIs between 1 and 10 years.
evidence: This describes the methods and participants of a cited study.

claim: Following cochlear implantation, participants' hearing sensitivity was between 30–40 dB HL (equivalent to a mild SNHL).
source: Following implantation, participants' hearing sensitivity was between 30–40 dB HL (i.e. equivalent to a mild SNHL)
evidence: This describes the hearing status of participants in Singh et al. (2004).

claim: None of the children with cochlear implants in Singh et al. (2004) showed a significant N1.
source: However, none of the children with CIs showed a significant N1
evidence: This describes findings from Singh et al. (2004).

claim: Only 10 (29%) of the children with cochlear implants in Singh et al. (2004) showed an MMN.
source: and only 10 (29%) showed an MMN.
evidence: This describes findings from Singh et al. (2004).

claim: Children with MMHL experience reduced and degraded auditory input, like children with severe-to-profound SNHL.
source: Like children with severe-to-profound SNHL, those with MMHL also experience reduced and degraded auditory input.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of hearing loss.

claim: The few studies that have assessed LAERs and MMRs for children with MMHL have yielded inconsistent results.
source: However, the few studies that have assessed LAERs and MMRs for children with MMHL have yielded inconsistent results.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: Rance et al. (2002) measured unaided P1-N1-P2 responses to speech and nonspeech sounds in 18, 3-to-9-year-old children with SNHL, of which five had MMHL.
source: Rance et al. (2002) measured unaided P1-N1-P2 responses to speech (synthesised /dæd/) and nonspeech (440 Hz pure tone) sounds in 18, 3-to-9-year-old children with SNHL, of which five had MMHL.
evidence: This describes the methods and participants of a cited study.

claim: All the children with MMHL in Rance et al. (2002) showed ERP responses to both speech and nonspeech stimulus types.
source: All the children with MMHL showed ERP responses to both stimulus types
evidence: This describes findings from Rance et al. (2002).

claim: The amplitude and latency of ERP responses in children with MMHL in Rance et al. (2002) did not differ from those of NH controls.
source: the amplitude and latency of which did not differ from those of NH controls.
evidence: This describes findings from Rance et al. (2002).

claim: Martinez et al. (2013) recorded the acoustic change complex (ACC) to changes in vowel height and place contrasts in five 2–6 year-old children with MMHL.
source: Martinez et al. (2013) recorded the acoustic change complex (ACC) to changes in vowel height and place contrasts in five 2–6 year-old children with MMHL.
evidence: This describes the methods and participants of a cited study.

claim: Robust and age-appropriate P1-N2 responses were observed in all but one of the children with MMHL in Martinez et al. (2013) whilst they were wearing their hearing aids.
source: Robust and age-appropriate P1-N2 responses were observed in all but one of the children with MMHL whilst they were wearing their hearing aids.
evidence: This describes findings from Martinez et al. (2013).

claim: Koravand et al. (2013) examined the effects of congenital MMHL on both the LAER and the MMN in children.
source: To our knowledge, only one study has examined the effects of congenital MMHL on both the LAER and the MMN in children (Koravand et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the scope of a cited study.

claim: The unaided ERPs of 12, 9–12 year-old children with MMHL were compared to those of 16 NH, age-matched controls in Koravand et al. (2013).
source: The unaided ERPs of 12, 9–12 year-old children with MMHL were compared to those of 16 NH, age-matched controls.
evidence: This describes the methods and participants of Koravand et al. (2013).

claim: All children in Koravand et al. (2013) showed P1 and N2 components.
source: Whereas all children showed P1 and N2 components
evidence: This describes findings from Koravand et al. (2013).

claim: N1 and P2 responses were absent in almost half of the children with MMHL in Koravand et al. (2013), compared to only a quarter of NH controls.
source: N1 and P2 responses were absent in almost half of the children with MMHL, compared to only a quarter of NH controls.
evidence: This describes findings from Koravand et al. (2013).

claim: The amplitude and latency of P1 and the MMN did not differ between children with MMHL and NH controls in Koravand et al. (2013).
source: The amplitude and latency of P1 and the MMN did not differ between children with MMHL and NH controls.
evidence: This describes findings from Koravand et al. (2013).

claim: Across all stimuli in Koravand et al. (2013), the N2 was significantly smaller (but not later) in children with MMHL.
source: However, across all stimuli, the N2 was significantly smaller (but not later) in children with MMHL.
evidence: This describes findings from Koravand et al. (2013).

claim: Koravand et al. (2013) concluded that reduced N2 amplitude may be a neurophysiological marker of central auditory processing deficits in children, including those with MMHL.
source: The authors concluded that reduced N2 amplitude may be a neurophysiological marker of central auditory processing deficits in children, including those with MMHL.
evidence: This describes the conclusion of Koravand et al. (2013).

claim: Where differences in LAERs have been reported for children with MMHL, these have been confined to older (9–12 year-old) rather than younger (2–9 year-old) children.
source: However, it is notable that where differences have been reported, these have been confined to older (9–12 year-old; Koravand et al., 2013) rather than younger (2–9 year-old; Rance et al., 2002; Martinez et al., 2013) children.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing findings across multiple cited studies.

claim: Delayed and diminished N1, N2, and MMN responses to speech sounds have been observed in adults with MMHL, particularly at lower stimulus intensities.
source: Interestingly, delayed and diminished N1, N2, and MMN responses to speech sounds have also been observed in adults with MMHL, particularly at lower stimulus intensities (Oates et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes findings from Oates et al. (2002).

claim: The effects of MMHL on the neural processing of sounds may only become apparent as children grow older.
source: One possible interpretation of these findings therefore is that, as for severe-to-profound SNHL (Ponton et al., 1996a; Ponton et al., 1996b; Ponton et al., 1999; Ponton et al., 2000b; Ponton and Eggermont, 2001), the effects of MMHL on the neural processing of sounds may only become apparent as children grow older.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pattern of findings across studies.

claim: At Time 1, the study measured the LAERs and MMRs evoked by simple nonspeech, complex speech-like nonspeech, and speech stimuli for 46, 8–16 year-old children with MMHL and 44 NH age-matched controls.
source: At Time 1, we measured the LAERs and MMRs evoked by simple nonspeech, complex speech-like nonspeech, and speech stimuli for 46, 8–16 year-old children with MMHL (MM group) and 44 NH age-matched controls (NH group).
evidence: This describes the methods of the current study.

claim: Stimuli were presented at a constant intensity of 70 dB SPL.
source: Stimuli were presented at a constant intensity of 70 dB SPL
evidence: This describes the methods of the current study.

claim: Children with MMHL were tested without their hearing aids in order to avoid stimulus alterations being introduced by the different hearing aid processors.
source: and children with MMHL were tested without their hearing aids in order to avoid stimulus alterations being introduced by the different hearing aid processors (Billings et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the rationale for a methodological choice in the current study.

claim: Children were divided into younger (Y; 8–11 years) and older (O; 12–16 years) age bands.
source: In order to evaluate developmental effects, children were divided into younger (Y; 8–11 years) and older (O; 12–16 years) age bands (see Table 1)
evidence: This describes the methods of the current study.

claim: There were no differences in audiometric thresholds between the Y and O children with MMHL.
source: There were no differences in audiometric thresholds between the Y and O children with MMHL (see Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the current study, supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Younger children with MMHL exhibited age-appropriate MMNs to all three stimulus conditions at Time 1.
source: However, whereas younger children with MMHL exhibited age-appropriate MMNs to all three stimulus conditions
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The MMN was absent in older children with MMHL at Time 1.
source: the MMN was absent in older children with MMHL.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: At Time 2 (+ 6 years), a subgroup (n = 13) of children from the MM-Y group from Time 1 was re-tested.
source: At Time 2 (+ 6 years), we re-tested a subgroup (n = 13) of children from the MM-Y group from Time 1.
evidence: This describes the methods of the longitudinal component of the study.

claim: At Time 2, the re-tested children were aged 13–17 years.
source: Owing to the time-lag between experiments, these children were now aged 13–17 years (i.e., they would now qualify for the MM-O group from Time 1).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of participants at Time 2.

claim: Despite showing age-appropriate MMNs at the group level when they were younger, children with MMHL showed no MMN to nonspeech or speech-like sounds six years later.
source: Despite showing age-appropriate MMNs at the group level when they were younger, these children showed no MMN to nonspeech or speech-like sounds six years later.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal component of the study.

claim: The findings suggest that MMHL in early-to-mid childhood leads to functional changes in auditory cortex that are predominantly reflected in the MMN.
source: Our findings therefore suggest that MMHL in early-to-mid childhood leads to functional changes in auditory cortex that are predominantly reflected in the MMN
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The functional changes in auditory cortex following MMHL only emerge during adolescence.
source: and that only emerge during adolescence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Regardless of group, children in the O age band were more likely to show a P2 than those in the Y age band.
source: In addition, regardless of group, children in the O age band were more likely to show a P2 than those in the Y age band [OR: 1.71, p=0.038].
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of the study data.

claim: Both the Y and O NH subgroups showed a significant MMN to large deviants in all three conditions at the group level.
source: At the group level, both the Y and O NH subgroups showed a significant MMN to large deviants in all three conditions
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MMN data.

claim: Both the Y and O NH subgroups showed a significant LDN to large deviants in the speech-like and speech conditions at the group level.
source: and a significant LDN to large deviants in the speech-like and speech conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of LDN data.

claim: The MM-Y subgroup showed a significant MMN to large deviants in all conditions at the group level.
source: Similarly, the MM-Y subgroup showed a significant MMN to large deviants in all conditions
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MMN data.

claim: The MM-Y subgroup showed a significant but brief MMN to small deviants in the nonspeech condition at the group level.
source: a significant but brief MMN to small deviants in the nonspeech condition
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MMN data.

claim: The MM-Y subgroup showed a significant LDN to large deviants in the speech-like and speech conditions at the group level.
source: and a significant LDN to large deviants in the speech-like and speech conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of LDN data.

claim: The MM-O subgroup failed to show a significant MMN to either large or small deviants in any of the three conditions at the group level.
source: However, contrary to their Y or NH peers, the MM-O subgroup failed to show a significant MMN to either large or small deviants in any of the three conditions
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of MMN data.

claim: The MM-O subgroup did not show an LDN to large or small deviants in the nonspeech or speech-like conditions at the group level.
source: or an LDN to large or small deviants in the nonspeech or speech-like conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of LDN data.

claim: The MM-O subgroup only showed a significant LDN to large deviants in the speech condition at the group level.
source: Rather, the MM-O subgroup only showed a significant LDN to large deviants in the speech condition.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of LDN data.

claim: Regardless of age band, children with MMHL were significantly less likely to show an MMN than NH children.
source: Regardless of age band, children with MMHL were significantly less likely to show an MMN than NH children [OR = 0.51, p=0.007].
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of MMN presence.

claim: There were no significant main effects or interactions for the LDN in terms of presence.
source: There were no significant main effects or interactions for the LDN.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of LDN presence.

claim: Only the main effect of condition was significant for MMN onset latency, with MMN onset earlier in the nonspeech condition than both the speech-like and speech conditions.
source: Only the main effect of condition was significant (χ(2)=39.69, p<0.001), with MMN onset earlier in the nonspeech condition than both the speech-like and speech conditions (both p<0.001), which did not differ from each other (p=0.863).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of MMN latency.

claim: There were no significant differences in variance of MMN onset latency for group, age band, or their two-way interaction.
source: There were no significant differences in variance for group, age band [both Fs <1, both ps >0.10], or their two-way interaction [F = 1.45, p=0.229].
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of MMN latency variability.

claim: For the MMN, the group × age band interaction contributed to the final model, just missing significance (p=0.069).
source: For the MMN, the group × age band interaction contributed to the final model, just missing significance (p=0.069).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of MMN amplitude.

claim: The NH-Y and MM-Y subgroups showed a small but non-significant difference in their MMN amplitudes.
source: Post-hoc t-tests indicated that whereas the NH-Y and MM-Y subgroups showed a small but non-significant difference in their MMN amplitudes [t(135.45)=−1.82, p=0.071, CI (−2.27, 0.09)]
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of MMN amplitude.

claim: The MM-O subgroup had significantly smaller MMNs than the NH-O subgroup.
source: the MM-O subgroup had significantly smaller MMNs than the NH-O subgroup [t(120.56)=−5.15, p<0.001, CI (−3.84,–1.71)] (see Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of MMN amplitude, supported by Figure 5.

claim: Difference wave amplitudes over the LDN time window did not differ between groups or age bands.
source: Difference wave amplitudes over the LDN time window did not differ between groups or age bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of LDN amplitude.

claim: Where present, P1 and P2 were slightly later (both by 11 ms) but not smaller in children with MMHL compared to NH controls, regardless of age.
source: Regardless of age, where present, P1 and P2 were slightly later (both by 11 ms; p=0.012, and p = .051, respectively) but not smaller (p=0.849 and p=0.468, respectively) in children with MMHL compared to NH controls.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of LAER component latencies and amplitudes.

claim: N2 was significantly smaller (by 2.67 µV) but not later in children with MMHL, regardless of age.
source: In contrast, N2 was significantly smaller (by 2.67 µV; p<0.001) but not later in children with MMHL (p = .482)
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of N2 amplitude and latency.

claim: The effect of smaller N2 in children with MMHL was greater in the speech-like condition than both the nonspeech and speech conditions.
source: an effect that was greater in the speech-like (p<0.001) than both the nonspeech and speech conditions (p=0.014 and p=0.002, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of N2 amplitude across conditions.

claim: Neither the amplitude or latency of the N1 differed between groups, where present.
source: Neither the amplitude or latency of the N1 differed between groups, where present (p>0.10).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of N1 amplitude and latency.

claim: Only around ¼ of children with MMHL showed an N1 or P2 response.
source: However, note that only around ¼ of children with MMHL showed an N1 or P2 response.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of component presence.

claim: For those individuals who showed a significant MMN to large deviants, the group × age band interaction for MMN amplitude again just missed significance (p=0.055).
source: For those individuals who showed a significant MMN to large deviants, the group × age band interaction for MMN amplitude again just missed significance (p=0.055).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of MMN amplitude for individuals with present MMNs.

claim: There was no significant group difference in MMN amplitude for the Y subgroups among individuals who showed a significant MMN.
source: Again, this was driven by the absence of a significant group difference for the Y subgroups [t(69.57)=−0.14, p=0.891, CI (−1.29, 1.13)]
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of MMN amplitude.

claim: Children in the MM-O subgroup had significantly smaller MMNs relative to their NH-O peers among individuals who showed a significant MMN.
source: in the presence of significantly smaller MMNs for children in the MM-O subgroup relative to their NH-O peers [t(48.46)=−3.20, p=0.002, CI (−3.01,–0.69)].
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of MMN amplitude.

claim: For the LDN, there were no differences between groups or age bands in the amplitude of the response where present.
source: For the LDN, there were no differences between groups or age bands in the amplitude of the response where present (p>0.10).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis of LDN amplitude for individuals with present LDNs.

claim: The LDN was only present in around ⅓ of children with MMHL.
source: However, again, the LDN was only present in around ⅓ of children with MMHL.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of LDN presence.

claim: Worse BEPTA thresholds were associated with reduced likelihood of presence of LAER components in all conditions for children with MMHL, although the effect was greater for the P1 and N2 than the N1 and P2 components.
source: For the LAER, worse BEPTA thresholds were associated with reduced likelihood of presence of components in all conditions, although the effect was greater for the P1 and N2 (both ps <1e−9) than the N1 and P2 components (both ps <10e−6).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis relating hearing thresholds to component presence.

claim: Worse BEPTA thresholds were associated with reduced likelihood of presence of an MMN for children with MMHL, consistent across age bands.
source: Worse BEPTA thresholds were also associated with reduced likelihood of presence of an MMN (p=0.020), but this was consistent across age bands.
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis relating hearing thresholds to MMN presence.

claim: For the LDN, there was a significant age band × BEPTA threshold interaction.
source: For the LDN, there was a significant age band ×BEPTA threshold interaction (p=0.039).
evidence: This is a finding from the statistical analysis relating hearing thresholds to LDN presence.

claim: Post-hoc logistic regressions conducted separately for each age band failed to reveal a significant effect of BEPTA on either the Y or O age bands for LDN presence.
source: However, post-hoc logistic regressions conducted separately for each age band failed to reveal a significant effect of BEPTA on either the Y (p=0.245) or O age bands (p=0.089).
evidence: This is a finding from post-hoc statistical analysis of LDN presence.

claim: For all conditions, the difference between both the large deviant and the standard and the small deviant and the standard was clearly detectable during pilot testing.
source: For all conditions, the difference between both the large deviant and the standard and the small deviant and the standard was clearly detectable during pilot testing (NH child listeners, n = 4).
evidence: This describes the stimulus validation.

claim: The difference between the large deviant and the standard was detectable during psychophysical testing by all but one child with MMHL in the cross-sectional study.
source: In addition, the difference between the large deviant and the standard was detectable during psychophysical testing by all but one child with MMHL in the cross-sectional study (the one with the highest BEPTA threshold; see Halliday et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the stimulus validation, supported by citation.

claim: EEG activity during audio presentation was recorded using a NuAmps 40-channel monopolar digital amplifier and NeuroScan 4.4 Acquire software system at a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
source: EEG activity during audio presentation was recorded using a NuAmps 40-channel monopolar digital amplifier and NeuroScan 4.4 Acquire software system (Neuromedical Supplies) at a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording method.

claim: The EEG was recorded from 28 scalp electrodes, positioned in the standard 10/20 configuration.
source: The EEG was recorded from 28 scalp electrodes, positioned in the standard 10/20 configuration.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording method.

claim: Additional electrodes were placed on the mastoids, and above and below the left eye (Vertical EOG) and on the outer canthi of both eyes (Horizontal EOG) to monitor eye movements.
source: Additional electrodes were placed on the mastoids, and above and below the left eye (Vertical EOG) and on the outer canthi of both eyes (Horizontal EOG) to monitor eye movements.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording method.

claim: Skin-to-electrode impedances were below 5 kΩ at the start of the recording and monitored to ensure they remained below 5 kΩ.
source: Skin-to-electrode impedances were below 5 kΩ at the start of the recording and monitored to ensure they remained below 5 kΩ.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording method.

claim: The EEG signal was amplified with a gain of 20000 and band-pass filtered at 0.1–70 Hz.
source: The EEG signal was amplified with a gain of 20000 and band-pass filtered at 0.1–70 Hz.
evidence: This describes the EEG recording method.

claim: EEG data were analysed offline using the EEGLAB toolbox and custom Matlab software.
source: EEG data were analysed offline using the EEGLAB toolbox (Delorme and Makeig, 2004) and custom Matlab software.
evidence: This describes the EEG analysis method.

claim: The EEG was filtered using an FIR band-pass filter at 0.5–35 Hz, and re-referenced to the averaged mastoids.
source: The EEG was filtered using an FIR band-pass filter at 0.5–35 Hz, and re-referenced to the averaged mastoids.
evidence: This describes the EEG analysis method.

claim: Data were epoched relative to stimulus onset using a −200 to 800 ms window and baseline corrected from −200 to 0 ms.
source: Data were epoched relative to stimulus onset using a −200 to 800 ms window and baseline corrected from −200 to 0 ms.
evidence: This describes the EEG analysis method.

claim: Epochs containing artefacts were rejected from the final averages on the basis of a ± 100 µV criterion for all channels.
source: Epochs containing artefacts were rejected (mean number rejected epochs across groups, age bands and conditions: 8.9 standards, 3.5 small deviants, 3.6 large deviants) from the final averages on the basis of a ± 100 µV criterion for all channels.
evidence: This describes the EEG analysis method.

claim: Individual epochs were averaged separately for each of the three conditions, and for standards and deviants.
source: Individual epochs were averaged separately for each of the three conditions, and for standards and deviants.
evidence: This describes the EEG analysis method.

claim: Standards directly following a deviant were excluded from the average.
source: Standards directly following a deviant were excluded from the average.
evidence: This describes the EEG analysis method.

claim: For each participant, the LAER components P1, N1, P2, and N2 at Cz that were evoked by the standards for each condition were identified by two independent judges.
source: For each participant, the LAER components P1, N1, P2, and N2 at Cz that were evoked by the standards for each condition were identified by two independent judges (including author OT).
evidence: This describes the method for identifying LAER components.

claim: A third judge made the final decision where there was disagreement between judges on LAER component identification.
source: A third judge (author AC) made the final decision where there was disagreement between judges.
evidence: This describes the method for identifying LAER components.

claim: All judges were experienced with clinical and research developmental EEG data.
source: All judges were experienced with clinical and research developmental EEG data.
evidence: This describes the qualifications of the judges.

claim: Cz was selected for LAER analysis because it was where responses were largest overall, as is typical for this sort of data.
source: Cz was selected because it was where responses were largest overall, as is typical for this sort of data (Ponton et al., 2000a).
evidence: This describes the rationale for electrode selection, supported by citation.

claim: Anonymized individual waveforms for each condition were presented to the judges, together with the grand-average NH waveform observed for the same condition for both the Y and O subgroups as a comparison point.
source: Anonymized individual waveforms for each condition were presented to the judges, together with the grand-average NH waveform observed for the same condition for both the Y and O subgroups as a comparison point.
evidence: This describes the method for presenting data to judges.

claim: Judges were blind to the participant group, age band, and stimulus condition for each waveform.
source: Judges were blind to the participant group, age band, and stimulus condition for each waveform.
evidence: This describes the blinding procedure.

claim: For a response to be considered present, at least two out of the three judges had to agree on the peak latency of each component in the individual waveform.
source: For a response to be considered present, at least two out of the three judges had to agree on the peak latency of each component in the individual waveform.
evidence: This describes the criterion for component presence.

claim: Consistency across the three judges reached 82% in the nonspeech condition, 74% in the speech-like condition, and 81% in the speech condition.
source: Consistency across the three judges reached 82% in the nonspeech condition, 74% in the speech-like condition, and 81% in the speech condition (consistency in line with those observed by Oates and Stapells, 1997).
evidence: This describes the inter-rater reliability, with comparison to a cited study.

claim: Voltage maps confirmed that the MMN was strongest in the fronto-central region (at around 200 ms post-stimulus onset), as is typical for this response.
source: Voltage maps confirmed that the MMN was strongest in the fronto-central region (at around 200 ms post-stimulus onset, see Figure 3), as is typical for this response (Näätänen et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the topography of the MMN, supported by a figure and citation.

claim: Statistical analyses for the MMN and LDN were conducted on data recorded at electrode Fz.
source: Statistical analyses for the MMN and LDN were therefore conducted on data recorded at electrode Fz.
evidence: This describes the electrode used for MMN/LDN analysis.

claim: To calculate the MMN/LDN, the responses evoked by standards were subtracted from responses evoked by deviants for each participant for each condition.
source: To calculate the MMN/LDN, the responses evoked by standards were subtracted from responses evoked by deviants for each participant for each condition.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating MMN/LDN.

claim: Differential waves were obtained separately for the small and large deviants.
source: Differential waves were obtained separately for the small and large deviants.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating MMN/LDN.

claim: For each group and age band, point-to-point comparison of the differential wave amplitudes was performed in order to determine the latency period over which the waveforms were significantly different from zero, if any.
source: First, for each group and age band, point-to-point comparison of the differential wave amplitudes was performed in order to determine the latency period over which the waveforms were significantly different from zero, if any.
evidence: This describes the method for assessing MMN/LDN presence at the group level.

claim: One-sided t-tests were computed within the 100–400 ms post-stimulus-onset time window for the MMN, with a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
source: One-sided t-tests were computed within the 100–400 ms post-stimulus-onset time window - identified as the region most likely to contain the MMN by visual inspection of the individual waveforms - with a sampling rate of 500 Hz.
evidence: This describes the statistical method for assessing MMN presence.

claim: The 400–600 ms time window was selected for the LDN.
source: The 400–600 ms time window was selected for the LDN.
evidence: This describes the time window for LDN analysis.

claim: An MMN/LDN was considered present when p<0.01 (one-tailed) for >20 ms at adjacent time-points at the group level.
source: Because adjacent points in the waveform are highly correlated potentially leading to spurious significant values in short intervals, an MMN/LDN was considered present when p<0.01 (one-tailed) for >20 ms at adjacent time-points (Kraus et al., 1993; McGee et al., 1997).
evidence: This describes the criterion for MMN/LDN presence at the group level, supported by citations.

claim: At the individual level, an MMN/LDN was considered present when p<0.05 (one-tailed) for >20 ms at adjacent time-points.
source: Next, this process was repeated at the individual level using the grand average waveforms obtained for each group, age band, and condition, with an ɑ level <0.05 (one-tailed) for >20 ms at adjacent time-points.
evidence: This describes the criterion for MMN/LDN presence at the individual level.

claim: Amplitude of the MMN was defined as the mean amplitude (in μV) in a 50-ms window centred around the NH-group grand-average peak latency for the appropriate age band, condition, and deviant type.
source: Amplitude of the MMN was defined as the mean amplitude (in μV) in a 50-ms window centred around the NH-group grand-average peak latency for the appropriate age band, condition, and deviant type (see Appendix 1—table 9).
evidence: This describes the method for calculating MMN amplitude.

claim: Amplitude of the LDN was defined as the mean amplitude (in μV) in a 50-ms window centred around each group's own grand-average peak latency in the given age band, condition and deviant type.
source: Therefore, amplitude of the LDN was defined as the mean amplitude (in μV) in a 50-ms window centred around each group's own grand-average peak latency in the given age band, condition and deviant type.
evidence: This describes the method for calculating LDN amplitude.

claim: A series of mixed-effects regression models was applied using the lme4 package of R.
source: A series of mixed-effects regression models was applied using the lme4 package of R (Bates et al., 2014).
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: Logistic mixed-effects regressions were conducted to determine whether group, age band, condition, component or response predicted the presence of a component/response.
source: Logistic mixed-effects regressions were conducted to determine whether group (NH vs. MM), age band (Y vs. O), condition (nonspeech, speech-like, and speech), component (P1, N1, P2, N2) or response (MMN or LDN) predicted the presence of a component/response.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: Linear mixed-effects regressions were conducted to determine whether group, age band, condition, or component predicted the amplitude or latency of components/responses.
source: Linear mixed-effects regressions were conducted to determine whether those same independent variables predicted the amplitude (P1-N2, MMN, and LDN) or latency (P1-N2 only) of these components/responses.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method.

claim: Starting from saturated models with listener as random intercepts, predictors were removed iteratively if their removal did not significantly worsen the fit of each model.
source: Starting from saturated models with listener as random intercepts, group, age band, condition, and component as main effects, and all two-, three- and four-way interactions included (which were treated as fixed-effect terms), predictors were removed iteratively if their removal did not significantly worsen the fit of each model.
evidence: This describes the model selection procedure.

claim: The most parsimonious models were selected using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).
source: The most parsimonious models were selected using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).
evidence: This describes the model selection criterion.

claim: Final models included only significant main effects and/or interactions, and Pseudo R2 (Nagelkerke) was used as an index of goodness-of-fit.
source: Final models included only significant main effects and/or interactions, and Pseudo R2 (Nagelkerke) was used as an index of goodness-of-fit.
evidence: This describes the final model characteristics.

claim: Six years later (Time 2), 14 children from the MM-Y group from Time 1 were successfully re-contacted and re-tested.
source: Six years later (Time 2), we attempted to re-contact all of the 23 children who initially constituted the MM-Y group from the cross-sectional study (at Time 1) and who had given their permission to be re-contacted at a future point in time. Fourteen of these children were successfully re-contacted, and all were re-tested 6 years after their initial participation (Time 2).
evidence: This describes the longitudinal follow-up procedure.

claim: Results from one child in the longitudinal study could not be included as their hearing had significantly deteriorated since Time 1.
source: Results from one child could not be included as their hearing had significantly deteriorated since Time 1.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for the longitudinal study.

claim: The remaining 13 children comprised the MM-YO group for the longitudinal study.
source: The remaining children (n = 13) comprised the MM-YO group for the longitudinal study.
evidence: This describes the composition of the longitudinal study group.

claim: The experimental setup for stimulus presentation and EEG recording at Time 2 was identical to that used at Time 1, with two main differences.
source: The experimental setup for stimulus presentation and EEG recording was identical to that used at Time 1, with two main differences.
evidence: This describes the methods for the longitudinal study.

claim: At Time 2, technical difficulties led to discarding EEG activity recorded on the left mastoids.
source: First, as the system was older, technical difficulties led to us to discard EEG activity recorded on the left mastoids.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference at Time 2.

claim: Data from the MM-YO subgroup was only re-referenced to the right mastoids at Time 2.
source: Therefore, data from the MM-YO subgroup was only re-referenced to the right mastoids.
evidence: This describes a methodological difference at Time 2.

claim: At Time 2, some scalp channels appeared consistently faulty, hence increasing the noise floor.
source: Second, some scalp channels appeared consistently faulty, hence increasing the noise floor at Time 2.
evidence: This describes a methodological issue at Time 2.

claim: Artefact rejection at Time 2 was limited to a threshold of ±100 µV criterion in either Cz or Fz.
source: Because the MMN typically displayed a fronto-central distribution for the cross-sectional study, we thus limited the artefact rejection to a threshold of ±100 µV criterion in either Cz or Fz.
evidence: This describes the artefact rejection method at Time 2.

claim: Data from the three other subgroups (MM-Y, MM-O, NH-O) were reprocessed using the same re-referencing and artefact rejection criterion as those applied to the MM-YO subgroup.
source: Data from the three other subgroups (MM-Y, MM-O, NH-O) were thus reprocessed using the same re-referencing and artefact rejection criterion as those applied to the MM-YO subgroup.
evidence: This describes the data reprocessing for consistency.

claim: There was no significant difference in noise floor between Time 1 and Time 2 studies in any of the three conditions.
source: There was no significant difference in noise floor between studies in any of the three conditions [nonspeech: χ2(12)=13.3, p=0.420; speech-like: χ2(12)=7.73, p=0.800; speech: χ2(12)=20.3, p=0.120].
evidence: This is a finding from comparing data quality between time points.
